Yuna: Daniel, I saw how well you looked after the children at the volunteering last weekend.
Daniel: Looked after them? Not at all. I only played with them.
Yuna: No — you soothed a crying child in no time, too. Every time I see you I think how patient you are. You must have been a kind big brother who looked after his little brother from childhood — right?
Daniel: Me? There's no way. To tell the truth, as a child I often made my brother cry.
Yuna: Really? Someone as warm as you are now can't have been like that.
Daniel: I was immature then. I was greedy, so when there were sweets I ate my brother's share too. He still says they were snatched from him the moment he opened the packet.
Yuna: Ha ha — then when did you change?
Daniel: When I was ten I was very ill, and my brother gave me all his sweets. That was the first time I felt ashamed.
Yuna: Your little brother was more grown-up than you.
Daniel: He was. So I am still repaying his kindness to this day.

Once upon a time a tiger lived deep in the mountains. One winter night the tiger, which had eaten nothing for several days, came down to a village looking for food. As it passed a house, it heard a baby crying inside.

Soothing the baby, the mother said, “If you keep crying, the tiger will come and carry you off.” Outside the door the tiger heard this and thought, ‘How did she know I had come? Now the baby will be frightened and stop crying.’ But far from stopping, the baby cried louder. The tiger was astonished. ‘There can't be a child that isn't afraid of me…’

Then the mother spoke again: “Here, look — a dried persimmon, a dried persimmon.” And the very moment she finished speaking, the baby stopped crying at once. The tiger's heart began to pound. ‘This Dried Persimmon must be a far more fearsome fellow than I am. I had better run before he eats me.’

The tiger ran to the mountains without once looking back. And after that, they say, it never came down to that village again.

Ladies and gentlemen, Korean old stories usually begin with the words “Once upon a time, in the days when tigers smoked pipes”. A tiger can't possibly smoke, can it? It means that this happened a very long time ago. As even this phrase shows, tigers appear often in Korean old stories.

The tiger in the stories comes in three guises. The first is the fearsome tiger: it tries to eat people and torments weaker animals. The second is the foolish tiger: it is strong but has no wit, so it is tricked by a rabbit or a fox and runs away, startled by the word “persimmon”. The third is the loyal tiger: it repays the kindness of someone who helped it and protects good people.

Then why does the tiger appear so often? It is said to be because, in this land of many mountains, the tiger was the animal people feared most. By making the fearsome tiger foolish in their stories and laughing, people tried to forget their fear. And through the tiger they also passed on the moral that if the strong torment the weak, they are punished in the end.

Once upon a time a traveller was walking along a mountain path. Then one day he heard a cry from somewhere: “Save me!” When he went to look, a tiger had fallen into a deep pit.

“Good traveller, please rescue me. I will certainly repay your kindness.”
“If I get you out, isn't it obvious that you'll eat me?”
“How could I do such a thing? I will never do that.”

The kind traveller lowered a long tree trunk into the pit. But the very moment the tiger was out of the pit, it sprang at the traveller. “Seeing food after three days, I can't hold back.”

The traveller asked a passing rabbit to judge who was right. Having heard the whole story, the rabbit said, “I can't really tell from words alone. Show me how things were at the start.” Saying “I was like this,” the tiger jumped down into the pit. At that the rabbit quickly removed the tree trunk and said, “Traveller, now go on your way. A tiger that knows no gratitude can stay right there.”

In the end, they say, the tiger that had not kept its promise found itself shut in the pit again.

Long ago Hwanin, the king of heaven, had a son called Hwanung. Looking down on the world from heaven, Hwanung took a liking to the land where people lived. Having obtained his father's leave, Hwanung came down to earth with the gods who rule wind, rain and cloud, and began to rule the people. He taught them how to farm and cured their illnesses.

At that time a bear and a tiger that lived in the same cave came to Hwanung and begged him to make them human. Giving them mugwort and garlic, Hwanung said, “If you eat these and do not see sunlight for a hundred days, you will become human.”

The bear and the tiger went into the cave. The tiger bore it well at first, but after a few days it could not stand the dark, stifling cave. In the end the tiger could not hold out and bolted from the cave. But the bear endured and waited to the end, and at last, after twenty-one days, it became a woman. People called this woman Ungnyeo.

Hwanung married Ungnyeo, and a son was born to them. This child is Dangun. Dangun founded a country at a place called Asadal and named it Joseon. This country is Gojoseon, which Koreans regard as their first state.

An **옛날이야기** is a folk tale told for pleasure, often to children. A **신화** (myth) tells of gods and of how the world or a country began. A **전설** (legend) is tied to a real place or person. The people and animals in a story are its **등장인물**.

**어리석다** — foolish, easily tricked. **영리하다** — clever, quick to learn. **겁이 많다** — easily frightened. **의리가 있다** — loyal: does not abandon a friend in trouble. **욕심이 많다** — wants more though he already has enough. **참을성이 많다** — bears pain or waiting without complaint. And the usual hero is simply **착하다** (good-hearted).

Four plots: someone helps you, and you **은혜를 갚다** (repay the kindness); someone does wrong and **벌을 받다** (is punished); someone **놀림을 당하다** (is teased — the passive of 놀리다 with 당하다); someone wronged **복수를 하다** (takes revenge).

**여우 같다** — clever at getting one's way, charming and sly. **곰 같다** — slow, and **눈치가 없다** (does not notice other people's mood). **호랑이 같다** — frightening when angry: 호랑이 선생님. **청개구리 같다** — a child who **말을 안 듣다** and does the opposite of what he is told. The last comes from a tale of a little green frog that always did the contrary of what its mother said.

A/V-(으)ㄹ 리(가) 없다 — it can't be

**리** means “reason, possibility”, so -(으)ㄹ 리가 없다 = “there is no possibility that…”: 점심을 **무료**로 **줄 리가 없어요** (they can't be giving lunch free). 그 사람이 거짓말을 **할 리가 없어요**. For something already done use **-았/었을 리가 없다**: 벌써 도착**했을 리가 없어요**. Noun: **N일 리가 없다** — **공짜일 리가 없어요**. On its own: **그럴 리가 없어요.**

The same meaning as a **rhetorical question**: 제 여자 친구가 여기에 **왔을 리가 있겠어요?** (how could my girlfriend have come here?). 아무리 학생이라도 밥을 공짜로 **줄 리가 있어요?** The answer expected is “of course not”. Compare the unit-4 pattern **-(으)ㄹ 게 뻔하다** (it is sure to be so): the two are opposite certainties.

One action follows another **so quickly that there is no gap**, usually because someone was waiting eagerly: 수업이 **끝나기가 무섭게** 나갔어요 (he left the moment class ended). 서점에 **진열하기가 무섭게** 다 팔려요. Verbs only; no tense ending on the first verb — the time is shown at the end. It is livelier than **-자마자**, and 가 is often dropped: 끝나기 무섭게.

N 만에 — after that much time

**만에** follows a length of time and says that something happened **when that much time had passed**: 뜨거운 라면을 1분 **만에** 다 먹었어요 (I ate it up in one minute). 며칠 **만에** 맛있는 음식을 먹었어요 (for the first time in days). 십 년 **만에** 친구를 만났어요. With 지: 한국에 온 **지** 일 년 **만에** 취직했어요. The set word **오랜만에** = after a long time.

**동안** = throughout a period: 삼 일 **동안** 잤어요 (I slept for three days). **만에** = at the end of a period, something happens once: 삼 일 **만에** 일어났어요 (I got up after three days). So 만에 goes with verbs of result — 끝내다, 만나다, 돌아오다, 고치다, 되다 — not with verbs of duration.

Begin: **옛날 옛날에** … -이/가 살았습니다. Turn the plot: **그러던 어느 날** (then one day). Close: **결국** … **-고 말았습니다** (ended up …ing — 3B) or **마침내** (at last, of something long awaited). And the storyteller's ending **-았/었답니다** (“…, so they say”): 다시는 내려오지 않았**답니다**.
Inside the story characters protest: **제가 그럴 리가 있겠습니까?** (how could I?) · **절대 -지 않을 거예요** (I will never…) · **-다니 말도 안 돼요** (that … is absurd). 절대 goes with a negative: 절대 잊지 않겠습니다.

Stories traditionally open “in the days when tigers smoked” — that is, very long ago. The tiger **등장하다** (appears) in three guises: fearsome, **어리석다** (tricked by a rabbit's **꾀**), and **의리가 있다** (repaying kindness). The weak animal that **속이다** (deceives) the strong one stands for **지혜** (wisdom), and each tale leaves a **교훈** (moral): whoever breaks a promise **벌을 받다**.

The **해치** (also called 해태) is a creature of **상상** — a legendary beast said to tell right from wrong, so it **상징하다** (symbolises) **정의** (justice); it is also believed to ward off fire and misfortune. Stone haechi stand before Gwanghwamun, the main gate of Gyeongbokgung Palace, and a pair stands at the National Assembly. In 2008 the city of Seoul chose the haechi as its symbol.
Pronunciation: an added ㄴ, then a nasal

When a word ending in a consonant is followed, inside a compound or phrase, by a word beginning with **이, 야, 여, 요, 유**, an ㄴ is added: 무슨 일 [무슨닐], 한여름 [한녀름]. If the consonant before it is ㄱ, ㄷ(ㅅ, ㅌ, ㅊ) or ㅂ, that consonant then becomes a nasal — ㄱ→[ㅇ], ㄷ→[ㄴ], ㅂ→[ㅁ]: 옛이야기 → 옏+니야기 → **[옌니야기]**; 한국 요리 → **[한궁뇨리]**.

When you eat in a Korean restaurant, there are times when the owner brings a dish you didn't order and says, “This is service.” A foreigner who hears this for the first time is easily flustered. The English word “service” means helping a customer, so one can't see why it is said while handing over food. In Korea the word is also used to mean “something given free, without taking money”.

Words like this, which come from English but are used differently from their original meaning or form, are called Konglish. There are several kinds. First, there are words whose meaning has changed, like seobiseu. Second, there are long words that have been shortened, like eeokeon (air conditioner) and rimokeon (remote control). Third, there are words newly made by joining English words, like haendeupon (“hand phone”, a mobile) and aisyoping (“eye shopping”). Looking round with one's eyes without buying is called aisyoping.

Not all loanwords come from English. Areubaiteu is originally a German word meaning “work”, but in Korea it means the short-hours jobs that students do. That this word is widely used can be seen from the fact that even a short form, alba, has arisen.

Konglish is sometimes mocked as wrong English. But for a word from another country to come in and change to fit the life of its new country is something one sees in any language.

Chair: Today we shall talk about using loanwords and foreign words in everyday life. Hayun, would you begin?

Listening to teenagers talking on a bus, one is sometimes startled. They are not angry and not quarrelling, yet a swear word is attached to the end of every phrase. Asked why they talk like that, most reply, “It's just a joke,” or “It's because we're close.” The idea is that, being a light joke, it does no harm. Does it really do no harm?

I think it does. First, because speech is habit. If you get into the way of swearing, the words come out without your knowing it even in situations where they must not be used. According to one secondary-school teacher, pupils who swear a lot when with friends have a hard time choosing their words when giving a presentation or practising for an interview.

Second, swear words take the place where other words would stand. If, glad or angry or surprised, one finishes with the same single word, there is no longer any need to look for the word that expresses one's feeling exactly. That one's power of expression grows poorer can easily be seen in such a person's writing.

Third, even if it was a joke to the speaker, the listener may be hurt. The meaning of a word is in many cases settled not by the one who speaks but by the one who hears.

Of course a single swear word does not change a person. But the words used every day become, little by little, that person's way of speaking, and the way of speaking becomes the impression that person makes. The reason not to swear is not that the words are bad words, but that the words I use in the end make me.
Kinds of words and what they do

**유행어** — a word or phrase everyone is saying this season; people **따라 하다** (copy) it. **외래어** — a loanword that has settled in Korean: 버스, 컴퓨터, 텔레비전; an **외국어** is a foreign language or a foreign word not yet settled. **줄임말** — a shortened word: 남친 (남자 친구), 알바 (아르바이트), 셀카. **욕** — swearing, abuse: 욕을 하다.

**-아/어 대다** — to keep doing something to excess, with a note of disapproval: 욕을 **해 대다**, 아이가 **울어 대다**, 옆집에서 **떠들어 대다**. **-아/어 버릇하다** — to do something so often that it becomes a habit: 줄임말을 **써 버릇하면** 원래 말을 잊어버려요. 늦게 **자 버릇해서** 아침에 못 일어나요.

Good: **친근한 느낌이 들다** (it feels friendly), **의사소통이 잘되다** (people understand one another), **표현이 풍부해지다** (there are more ways to say things). Bad: **대화가 끊기다** (the talk breaks off because someone can't follow), **오해가 생기다** (a misunderstanding arises), **기분이 상하다** (someone is hurt).

**-력** (力) means “power, ability”: **표현력** (of expression), **이해력** (of understanding), **어휘력** (command of words), **상상력** (imagination), **기억력** (memory). They are **뛰어나다** (outstanding) or **부족하다** (lacking); only 기억력 is usually **좋다 / 나쁘다**. For their pronunciation see lesson 4.

At both the northern and the southern end of the earth there is ice. But the ice in the two places is different. In the middle of the Arctic there is no land: the Arctic ice is ice floating on the sea. The Antarctic, by contrast, has a wide land, and on that land lies thick ice of more than two kilometres on average.

What happens when the Arctic ice shrinks through global warming? First, the creatures that live there lose their home. The polar bear catches its prey on the sea ice. When the ice melts and disappears, the polar bear loses even the place where it finds food. Warming also speeds up, because white ice reflects sunlight whereas the dark sea absorbs it. The more the ice shrinks, the more heat the sea takes in, and that heat in turn melts the ice.

Then why does the sea level rise? Just as the water does not overflow when the ice in a glass melts, ice floating on the sea hardly changes the height of the sea when it melts. What matters is the ice on land. When Antarctic ice melts and runs into the sea, the sea water grows by that much. It is said that if all the ice of the Antarctic melted, the sea level would be about sixty metres higher than now.

Of course, for all the Antarctic ice to melt may be a matter of the distant future. But even if only part of it melts, low land on the coast can be submerged. Climate change is not the polar bears' problem alone but that of the countless people who live by the sea. What shall we do? It is a question to be answered before it is too late.

Last weekend I went to Sol Island alone. The moment three months of being busy day and night with work ended, I packed my bag. Rather than rest at home, I wanted to walk somewhere nobody knew me.

On Sol Island there is a trail that goes once round the island. Unlike other tourist spots, this path has no shops and no announcements. You simply keep the sea on your left and walk. For the first half hour thoughts of the office came ceaselessly. But when I had passed the pine wood and stood on the hill, the endlessly stretching sea came into view all at once, and at that moment my head cleared.

Halfway along the path stands the “wishing tree”: a tree on which travellers hang small wooden tags with their wishes written on them. Countless tags swayed in the wind and made a sound. I stood for a long while without a word, reading other people's wishes. A family's health, passing an examination, the success of a first shop… They were not very different from mine. Since I was there, I wrote one too and hung it up.

It took about four hours to walk the whole trail. My legs ached, but my mind had grown calm. Perhaps true travel is not going far but stepping out of everyday life for a moment and looking back at oneself.

Eunpo is a small port town that lacks nothing, be it things to see or things to eat. The town is not large, so it can be seen perfectly well on foot. From Seoul it takes about four hours by express bus.

[To see] Eunpo harbour and the mural alley
Ten minutes' walk from the bus terminal brings you to Eunpo harbour. Seeing the fishing boats standing in a row under a sky where seagulls fly, one grows calm. On the hill behind the harbour is the mural alley. Unlike a big tourist spot, it is an alley where residents actually live, so one must walk quietly.

[To see] The Moon-viewing observation point
From the observation point at the top of the hill, the sea off Eunpo and its small islands can be seen at a glance. The sunset is especially beautiful. Having climbed as far as the observation point, we recommend walking just ten minutes more to the lighthouse as well.

[To eat] Eunpo market
In the market you can buy fresh seafood landed that morning. Eunpo's speciality is anchovy noodles. Unlike the noodles of other regions, the broth is very clear and there is almost no garnish. While you are looking round the market, it is good to try a bowl.

[Lodging] Guest houses
Near the harbour there are many guest houses. Rather than book the expensive hotel in front of the station, it is better to stay in a guest house with a view of the sea. If you ask the owner, he will tell you the time of the morning sunrise.

[Getting there] Sol Island
If you have time, go to Sol Island too. The ferry runs three times a day and takes about forty minutes. It does not run on very windy days, so you must check beforehand.

V-느니 (차라리) — rather than that, I'd sooner

Of **two unwelcome choices, the second is the lesser evil**: 주말에 사람 많은 곳에 가**느니 차라리** 집에 있는 게 낫다 (rather than go somewhere crowded, I'd sooner stay at home). 이 시간에 버스를 타**느니 차라리** 걸어가겠어요. Stem + **-느니**, verbs only, no tense; the second half ends in **-는 게 낫다 / -겠다 / -(으)ㄹ래요**. **차라리** (“rather”) may be left out but is usual.

**-는 것보다** simply compares: 버스를 타는 것보다 걷는 게 빨라요. **-느니** adds feeling: the first choice is so disagreeable that even the second, itself no pleasure, is preferable — 김빠진 콜라를 마시**느니** 차라리 물을 마시겠어요. So it sounds strong; do not use it of someone's kind offer.

**달리** is the adverb of 다르다. N**과/와 달리** = “differently from N, unlike N”: 저는 형**과 달리** 수영에 **소질**이 없어요 (unlike my brother, I have no gift for swimming). 다른 지역**과 달리** 이 지역에서는 휴대 전화가 잘 안 된다. With a clause: 지난번에 갔을 때**와 달리** **관람객**이 많았다. 생각했던 것**과 달리** …. After a consonant **과**, after a vowel **와**.

4A unit 3 **N에 비해(서)** — measured against N. 4A unit 4 **-(으)ㄴ/는 반면에** — whereas. Unit 11 **N치고** — for an N. **N과/와 달리** — unlike N; it states a plain difference and is common in guidebooks and self-introductions: 저는 보기와 달리 ….

Many people think that numbers are no more than simple signs for counting things. Yet people like some numbers and avoid others. The feeling for numbers differs from country to country.

In Korea, 3 has been regarded as a good number since old times. There is the word samsebeon, meaning that whatever it is, one should try three times, and in rock-paper-scissors too it is often the one who wins two games out of three who wins. To someone who has failed once people even say, “It's three goes, so try again.” It is felt to be fair only when there are three chances.

By contrast, 4 is a number that is avoided. This is because sa, the sound of the number 4 read as a Chinese character, is the same as the sa that means “to die”. So there are buildings whose lifts show the English letter F in place of the fourth floor, and some hospitals have no fourth floor or room number four. People's feeling for numbers has, one may say, been reflected in real life.

Of course, many people nowadays do not believe in such things. Living on the fourth floor does not mean that something bad will happen. Even so, the wish to choose a good number if one can on an important day — that too may be called a part of culture.

Good day. I shall present the results of our class survey. Last week our group put the question “What impresses you most about life in Korea?” to forty level-4 students of our language school.

The survey showed that the students who answered “fast delivery” numbered sixteen, accounting for forty per cent of the whole, and came first. Many said they were surprised that, on top of an order arriving quickly even late at night, there is hardly any food that cannot be delivered. Next in order came “convenient public transport” with ten and “24-hour convenience stores” with eight. “Other” was six — no more than fifteen per cent.

The answers differed according to how long the student had lived in Korea. Students who had been in Korea less than six months answered mainly delivery and convenience stores, whereas those who had lived here a year or more often answered public transport.

From this result it would seem that the students of our class are more impressed by the conveniences of life they experience every day than by old sites or traditions. However, since only forty students of one class were surveyed, we cannot say that this is what all foreigners think. That is all.

Only thirty per cent of students read books (an invented article)
Last month the student council of Saebyeol University carried out a questionnaire survey on reading habits among two hundred enrolled students. The survey showed that the students who answered that they read one or more books a month numbered sixty — no more than thirty per cent of the whole. The answer “I read now and then” was the commonest, with ninety (forty-five per cent), and the answer “I do not read at all” also accounted for fifty (twenty-five per cent).

As to the reason for not reading, over half the students answered “because I have no time”. That is, on top of having many classes they even have to do part-time work, so there is no time to read. Yet in the same survey the students answered that they use their mobile phones four hours a day on average. That makes twenty-eight hours a week, so it amounts to spending more than one day in seven looking at a phone.

Reading time also differed according to year. First-year students turned out to read two books a month on average, but fourth-year students did not reach even one. It appears that reading time shrank as preparation for employment began.

The student council said that, in accordance with the results of this survey, it plans to set up a “twenty minutes of reading a day” group from next term. A member of the council said, “Having no time is no more than part of the reason,” adding, “If a friend who reads is beside you, reading time will grow too.”

The five verbs of a survey report, in order: N을/를 **대상으로 조사하다** (to survey N) → …는지에 대해 **질문하다** (to ask whether…) → …다고 **응답하다** (to answer that…) → …다는 대답이 N을/를 **차지하다** (answers that… account for N) → …(으)ㄴ/는 것으로 **나타나다** (it turns out that…). A written survey is a **설문 조사**; its outcome is the **결과**.

Of numbers in general: **증가하다 / 늘어나다** (to increase) ↔ **감소하다 / 줄어들다** (to decrease) — the first of each pair is the written word. Of prices and pay: **인상되다 / 오르다** (to go up) ↔ **인하되다 / 내리다** (to come down). The particles: 5퍼센트**가** 올랐다 · 5퍼센트**나** 올랐다 (as much as) · 100명**에서** 80명**으로** 줄었다.

**률 / 율** (率) means “rate”: **확률** (probability), **인상률** (rate of increase), **경쟁률** (competition ratio — 경쟁률이 5 대 1이다), **환율** (exchange rate), **할인율** (discount rate), **비율** (proportion). It is written **율** after a vowel or ㄴ (비율, 환율, 할인율) and **률** after any other consonant (확률, 인상률, 경쟁률). For how these are pronounced, see lesson 4.
**평균** (average): 하루 평균 네 시간. **절반** (half): 절반을 넘다 / 절반에 못 미치다. **비율** (proportion): 남녀 비율. **퍼센트**: 30퍼센트 — in speech also 프로. **N명 중(에서) N명**: 스무 명 중 열 명.

Something **varies as N varies**: 지역**에 따라서** 집값에 차이가 있어요 (house prices differ by region). 거리**에 따라** 지하철 **요금**이 달라요. 나이**에 따라** 생각이 다르다. The sentence usually ends in **다르다 / 달라지다 / 차이가 있다**. With a question word clause: 어떻게 하느냐**에 따라** 결과가 달라진다. A second meaning, “in accordance with”: 조사 결과**에 따라** 계획을 바꿨다.

**N마다** = “each N” (level 2): 사람**마다** 생각이 달라요. **N에 따라** names the **factor** that explains the difference: 나이에 따라, 성별에 따라, 경험에 따라. Often both are possible; 에 따라 is the one for reports and explanations.

You **pile a second fact on the first**, and both point the same way — both good or both bad: 성격이 **쾌활한 데다가** 유머도 있어요 (cheerful, and witty into the bargain). **물가**가 **인상된 데다가** 기름값까지 올랐어요. At gatherings Koreans play number games. In **삼육구 (3·6·9)** everyone sits in a circle and counts up in turn to a **박자** (beat): 1, 2 … but on any number containing 3, 6 or 9 you do not say it — you **박수를 치다** (clap) instead. Once upon a time — no, it was only yesterday. In a park in the very middle of the city a meeting of the animals was held.

First the pigeon spoke. “People keep throwing us biscuits. At first that was nice. But from eating nothing but biscuits our bodies have grown heavy, and now we fly less well than we used to. As birds, we want to fly in the sky.”

The cat spoke. “I was bought because I was pretty, and thrown out because I was a nuisance. I am not a toy but a living animal.”

The dog spoke too. “My master loves me. But when I am alone in the house all day I am very lonely. And if I bark, I am scolded for being noisy.”

All were angry and shouted, “Let us drive the people out of the park!” Then an old magpie up in a tree spoke.
“Instead of just being angry, let us think carefully. It was a person, too, who took me to hospital yesterday when I was hurt. It is not because people are bad that they act so, but because they do not know us well. Therefore, instead of driving them out, we must let them know what kind of animals we are.”

The animals thought for a long while and then put up a notice at the park gate: “We are your neighbours. Please do not feed us, and take us in as family only when you can be responsible to the end.”

The dodo was a bird that lived on the island of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean. Though a bird, the dodo could not fly. Since there were no animals on the island to threaten the dodo and food enough on the ground, it had no reason to flee. As long ages passed, the dodo seems to have evolved towards losing the unneeded ability to fly.

But when Dutch sailors reached the island in 1598, a crisis came upon the dodo's peaceful life. Since the dodo had never seen people, it was not afraid of them and did not run away. The sailors, hungry after a long voyage, caught and ate dodos recklessly.

A greater problem was the animals that people brought to the island. The rats, pigs, dogs and others that came by ship ate up the eggs and young of the dodo in their nests on the ground. Since the dodo is said not to have laid many eggs at a time, its numbers must have shrunk fast. The last reliable record of a dodo being seen is from 1662. Less than a hundred years after people came to the island, the dodo had become extinct.

The story of the dodo is not merely the story of one bird on one island. As the event that first showed that human actions can make another living thing disappear for ever, it is still often told. Protecting the animals and plants that are in danger of extinction today is in order not to make a second dodo.

The passing of parents' bodily features to their children is called heredity. We inherit from our parents many features, such as the colour of our eyes and hair and the shape of our face, and those features are passed on again to the next generation.

The form of the hair, too, is influenced by heredity. So it often happens that a curly-haired child is born to curly-haired parents. But there are also cases in which both parents have straight hair and the child has curly hair. This is because most features are determined not by one gene but by several.

The ability to roll the tongue was for a long time given in textbooks as an example of a feature fixed by heredity. But it came to light that even among identical twins, whose genes are the same, there are cases in which only one can roll the tongue. There are also people who came to be able to roll it by practising. Therefore this ability should be seen not so much as determined by heredity alone as influenced by heredity and practice together.

It is the same with height. Height is greatly influenced by the genes inherited from one's parents, but it also differs according to the environment — what one ate and how one grew up. What we look like is the joint work of heredity and environment.

Watching a science-fiction film or reading such a novel, have you ever thought, “Surely such a thing can't be possible”? Yet of the technologies that appeared in works of the past, not a few are things we now use every day.

In a French novel that came out in the nineteenth century there is a story of people going to the moon. People of that time will have taken it only as an amusing fancy. But about a hundred years after that, people really went to the moon.

In old science-fiction films there are often scenes of talking with someone far away while seeing the person's face on a screen. There are also scenes of working a machine by touching a screen with the hand, or of giving orders by voice. To the audiences who marvelled at such scenes, these were matters of a distant future. But now even children make calls on a mobile telephone while seeing each other's faces, and at home a cleaning robot goes about by itself.

Of course not every fancy in the films has become reality. There are things, such as time travel, that still look impossible. Yet a new technology, before it is made by the hands of scientists, is first born in someone's imagination. Imagination is not so much a useless thing as a force that advances science. It would be amusing, too, to predict which scene in the films we watch today will become the reality of the future.

The first lotion makes the bonds **끊어지다**; the hair is rolled; the second lotion joins them again in the new shape, so the wave is **유지하다**-ed. **Washing**: **세제** clings to the **때** and loosens it from the cloth, and the moving water carries it away.

**상식** is what everyone “knows”. Science begins when you **의심하다** it. A famous example: the story that water leaving a **세면대** turns one way in the **북반구** and the other in the **남반구** because the Earth **돌다**. In fact that force is far too weak in a basin; the **방향** is decided by the basin's shape and the water's first motion. Only in something as big as a **태풍** does the Earth's turning show.
Culture: the sundial and the water clock

Both were made in 1434, in the reign of King Sejong. **앙부일구**, a **해시계**, is a bowl like a cauldron facing the sky: the tip of the **그림자** shows the hour, and lines across the bowl show the **계절** — a clock and a calendar in one. It was set up where ordinary people could see it. **자격루**, a **물시계** made by Jang Yeong-sil and others, measured time by flowing water and then, by itself, struck a bell, a drum and a gong (**종이 울리다**); it served as the kingdom's standard clock.

Time: long ago / Place: a certain village
Characters: Narrator, Nolbu, Heungbu, Heungbu's wife, the children, a swallow

Narrator: Long ago, in a certain village, there lived two brothers called Nolbu and Heungbu. The elder, Nolbu, was greedy and nasty by nature, but the younger, Heungbu, was good-hearted. When their father died, Nolbu took all the property for himself.

Nolbu: (coming out into the yard, loudly) Heungbu! With so large a family, how long do you mean to keep eating in my house? Get out this very day!
Heungbu: (bowing his head) I understand, brother. Thank you for everything.

Narrator: Heungbu's family came to live in a little hut at the foot of the hill. They worked hard, but were always poor.

Children: (clutching their stomachs) Father, we're hungry! Give us rice, rice!
Heungbu's wife: The children keep begging like that, and we haven't a handful of rice — what are we to do?
Heungbu: I'll go to my brother and borrow just a little. Surely he wouldn't turn a blind eye?

Narrator: But Heungbu, far from getting rice, was only scolded, and came plodding back. One spring day a swallow that lived under Heungbu's roof fell to the ground.

Children: Father, the swallow's leg is broken!
Heungbu: (lifting the swallow in both hands) Oh dear, how it must hurt. Bear it just a little. I'll mend it for you. (He binds the leg well with cloth.)

Narrator: The swallow, its leg healed, flew freely away to the south when autumn came.

Narrator: The next spring, that swallow came back.

Swallow: (circles round and round above the yard, then drops a seed.)
Children: Father, the swallow has dropped something!
Heungbu: (picking it up and looking) Why, it's a gourd seed. It seems to have brought it to repay our kindness. Let us plant it.

Narrator: When summer had passed, great gourds hung in clusters on the roof.

Heungbu's wife: Husband, the gourds are quite ripe. Let's pick one, boil and eat the inside, and use the shell as a bowl.
Heungbu: Let's. Now, all take hold of the saw together.
Heungbu's family: (sawing) Gently, gently, let us saw! Gently, gently, let us saw!

(With a “pop” the gourd splits and rice pours out.)

Children: Rice! Rice is pouring out!
Heungbu's wife: Gracious, this isn't a dream, is it?
Heungbu: Let's open the other gourds too.

(From the second gourd pours money, from the third silk.)

Narrator: Each time they opened a gourd, rice, money, silk — all kinds of treasure — came pouring out. Heungbu's family, beaming, shared their rice with the neighbours. The news soon reached Nolbu's ears too.

Narrator: Hearing that Heungbu had become rich, Nolbu came running.

Nolbu: Heungbu, how did you become rich overnight? Tell me the truth!
Heungbu: I mended a swallow whose leg was broken, and the swallow brought me a gourd seed.
Nolbu: (to himself) Just so — I need only do the same.

Narrator: As soon as Nolbu got home he caught a swallow and broke its leg on purpose. Then, binding it with cloth, he said:

Nolbu: I have mended you, so be sure to bring a gourd seed next spring. A big one!

Narrator: The next spring the swallow did indeed drop a gourd seed and go. When autumn came, gourds grew on Nolbu's roof too.

Nolbu: (beaming) Wife, bring the saw quickly. Treasure will come out!
Nolbu and his wife: (sawing in haste) Quickly, quickly, let us saw! Quickly, quickly, let us saw!

(With a “pop” the gourd splits and goblins leap out.)

Goblin: You wretch, Nolbu! You drove out your brother and even broke a swallow's leg — take your punishment! (They vanish with everything in the house.)
Nolbu: (trembling all over) Oh, I did wrong! Spare me!

Narrator: Nolbu lost everything overnight. Hearing the news, Heungbu came running.

Heungbu: Brother, do not worry. At our house there are rooms, rice, everything — let us live together.
Nolbu: (shedding tears) Heungbu, I did wrong. Forgive me.

Narrator: Nolbu repented of the past and became a good man. After that, it is said, the two brothers helped each other and lived happily for a long, long time.

The action is **repeated or carried too far**, and the speaker usually **does not like it**: 옆 사람들이 계속 떠들**어 대는** 바람에 제대로 못 봤어요 (they kept on chattering). 아기가 **밤새** 울**어 대서** 한숨도 못 잤어요. 아이들이 배고프다고 졸**라 대요**. Verbs only. Typical partners: 계속, 자꾸, 하루 종일, 밤새, 하도.

Like -아/어 보다: ㅏ, ㅗ → **-아 대다** (놀다 → 놀아 대다); other vowels → **-어 대다** (먹다 → 먹어 대다); 하다 → **해 대다** (전화하다 → 전화해 대다). Irregulars change as usual: 조르다 → 졸라 대다, 부르다 → 불러 대다, 묻다 → 물어 대다. Very often it leads to a result: **-아/어 대서 / 대는 바람에 / 대니까**.

Not with adjectives (~~예뻐 대다~~), not for a single act (~~한 번 물어 대다~~), and not of what you admire: of a hard-working friend say 열심히 공부해요, not 공부해 대요 — that would sound as though his studying annoyed you. Of oneself it is used with a rueful smile: 어제 과자를 너무 먹어 댔더니 배가 아파요.

Reading a play: Heungbu and Nolbu

A **대본** begins with **때** (time), **곳** (place) and **나오는 사람** (characters). The **해설자** tells what the audience cannot see. Each **대사** follows the speaker's name and a colon. Words in brackets are stage directions — how to speak or move: (큰 소리로), (고개를 숙이며), (톱질을 하며). Each **장면** is one piece of the action; each actor has a **역할**.

Elders in old tales speak down with **-느냐? / -(으)냐?** (questions), **-거라 / -너라** (commands: 나가**거라**, 가져오**너라**), **-(으)마** (a promise: 고쳐 주**마**), **-로구나** (discovery: 박 씨**로구나**). The younger answers with -습니다 and **형님**. The sawing chant **-세** means “let us”: 톱질하**세**. You need only recognise these.

Culture: the tale of the two brothers

**흥부와 놀부** is one of the best-known Korean folk tales, and it is also sung as a **판소리** — a long story performed by one singer with a drummer. Its lesson is that a good heart is rewarded and greed punished. To this day a spiteful, grudging temper is called 놀부 심보, and the **제비** that returns in spring is a bringer of good news.
